title: Chalcedon (451)
hookLine: one person, two natures; some ancient churches did not accept the wording, and dialogue continues today

lines: WHO IS JESUS, IN ONE SENTENCE?
cards: How do you say, in one sentence, who Jesus is? Bishops have argued over it for a long time, and now they're gathered at Chalcedon, a city just across the water from Constantinople, to try again. The question is sharp.
If Jesus is truly God, is he really human, with a human mind and a human tiredness? If he's truly human, how is he God? One side fears a Christ split in two.
The other fears a Christ blended into something neither. Whole churches are listening.

teach.b: The council's answer is short to say and hard to live inside. One and the same Christ, its definition says, truly God and truly human.
Known in two natures, without confusion, without change, without division, without separation. Two natures, one person.
These words work like fences around a mystery. They don't explain how. They mark where not to go: don't blend the two into a mixture; don't split him into two people sharing a body.
Behind it stands a line from John's Gospel, in the King James: "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us."

teach.h: SOME CHURCHES DID NOT ACCEPT IT.
teach.b: Catholic and Eastern Orthodox churches, and the Protestant churches that hold the early creeds, accept the Chalcedonian definition. But not everyone did.
Some ancient churches, the Coptic, the Armenian, the Ethiopian and the Syriac Orthodox among them, did not accept the wording. They were not denying that Christ is fully God and fully human.
They preferred to speak of one united nature of God the Word made flesh, from two, and to them two natures sounded like splitting him. Today these churches are often called the Oriental Orthodox.

The parting was real, it hurt, and it lasted. But the talking never fully stopped. In recent times, leaders and theologians from both sides have met, and some have said they confess the same Christ in different words.

Full communion hasn't been restored; the conversation continues. So Chalcedon is two things at once: a definition the churches that accept it hold dear, and a parting people on both sides are still tending.
And both sides still confess the same short line: truly God, truly human.

how: Churches that accept Chalcedon teach Christ as one person in two natures; Oriental Orthodox churches (Coptic, Armenian, Ethiopian, Eritrean, Syriac and Malankara) confess one united nature of the incarnate Word, and the two families of churches continue in dialogue.

o: the city where Augustine wrote The City of God
the council that first wrote the Nicene Creed
the council that said Christ is one person, two natures

games.q: who says what — tap the pairs.

s: the churches that did not accept Chalcedon deny that Christ is human
they confess Christ fully God and fully human. they objected to the wording.
Chalcedon explains exactly how Christ is both God and human
its words mark boundaries, without confusion, without division, more than they explain how.
the conversation between the churches continues today
full communion hasn't been restored, but leaders and theologians keep meeting.

games.q: you lead a church that treasures the words one nature of God the Word made flesh. the council says two natures. what do you do?
o: sign the wording anyway, to keep the peace.
keep your own wording: one united nature, from two.
stop saying anything about who Christ is.
games.why: some ancient churches kept their own wording, while confessing Christ fully God and fully human. the parting lasted, and the dialogue continues.

practice: If you pray, pray for the churches that parted after Chalcedon and for the people still talking: Coptic, Armenian, Ethiopian, Syriac, and the churches on the other side of the table.

If you don't, bring to mind a split you know, in a family, a friendship, a group that used to be one, and notice that each side may have been guarding something true. Hold both sides in quiet goodwill.

wordCard.voice: Chalcedon. The council that said Christ is one person in two natures, and the parting of churches that followed.

orig.note: Greek: nature. the word at the center of the argument: two natures, or one united nature.

carryVoice: Your line: truly god, truly human. One Christ, confessed in different words. See you tomorrow.
